tells: Opens by picking up the previous idea ('A light placed in one heart can reach another and this, for Sheikh Bahmanpour, is...'), semicolon-joined contrast, quotation attributed then glossed; plain 'we' register.

Epigraph gloss in A's flat manner ('These words come near the end of...', 'many of us hear it'), cross-reference to an earlier chapter's question, closes with a plain statement of what the chapter does.

Concrete homely analogy explained in one line ('A person does not try to understand their hunger; they arrive at it and feel it'), like the red-light and rusted-machine images; 'he says' mid-sentence; a working distinction stated then qualified.
Stacked short quotations each introduced by 'he writes / He adds / he goes on / In another place', exactly the Tabatabaʾi paragraph pattern; paragraphs link back to the prologue line.

'Let's start with the two kinds of knowing' mirrors 'Let's start with two claims'; 'The Arabic for a definition, hadd, also means a limit' mirrors 'The Arabic for "brought near" is muqarrabun'; Sheikh's point drawn out from the word.
'it is the law lived from the inside' — a tidy aphorism closing a thought; Author A would state it plainly ('the path stays inside the law') and move on
'A fear that mysticism might do exactly that' — spoken emphasis; A would write 'A fear that mysticism might do so'
'each chapter and the epilogue offer small, practical steps for bringing this into daily life' — blurb-like promise to the reader; A describes what the text argues, not what it offers
'a reader should feel able to say what ʿirfan is and is not' — presumes the reader's feelings; A keeps to the argument
'Let's take them in turn' and a numbered sequence ('The first is sight...'), the faculty-behind-the-eyes argument restated plainly, quotation explained through 'Sheikh Bahmanpour explains why'.

Quotation introduced, then 'The next sentence of the oration gives the reason'; 'Reason is not left with nothing to do' picks up the last point; objection raised and answered flatly ('Sheikh Bahmanpour does not draw that conclusion').
'And it ends not in withdrawal from the world but in return' — sentence opening with 'And' in an anaphoric run ('It is rooted... It is walked... And it ends'); A does not build rhetorical crescendos
'some of the words you'll meet' — contraction and direct 'you'; A writes 'we' or impersonal
'Additional call-out sections are spread throughout with helpful context and short side notes' — publisher's-blurb diction ('helpful'); A never sells the book to the reader
'a welcoming introduction to ʿirfan, a guide to beginning the journey that strives for brevity and clarity' — self-description in grand abstract nouns; A states the claim and the evidence

'Let's start with the order in which the prayers ask'; Arabic term given and glossed ('inqitaʿ, being cut off'); Sheikh's question reported and answered in two flat clauses ('In the heart, he answers, it is'); link back to Chapter One.
'asks why a believer should bother' — informal spoken phrasing; A would write 'asks why a believer should seek more than the obligations'
'with a compatible view of similarities to Sufism' — vague abstract stacking; A names the point concretely

'the boundary that keeps the traveller safe: the shariʿa' / 'passes through on the journey towards ʿirfan: the self' — repeated colon-reveal flourish; A uses colons for lists and explanations, not for suspense

Opens by carrying the previous point forward ('Knowledge that analysis cannot produce has to come from somewhere else'); hadith explained clause by clause; a possible misreading raised and handed to the Sheikh's own words.
'One addresses the heart of the seeker, the other the eye of the one choosing a guide' — tidy antithesis with unclear referents as a closing summary; A would name who is meant and avoid the epigram
'For him the feats are beside the point: something a student should look past' — colon used to append a loose gloss; A writes a full second sentence

Paragraph starts by restating a conclusion already reached ('Sheikh Bahmanpour calls such powers shirk and Mutahhari's words show why') and then switches subject to judging a teacher mid-paragraph; A keeps one step per paragraph
'Here is the passage the wedding verse belongs to' — spoken presenter's phrasing; A would write 'The verse belongs to a passage in Surah al-Rum'

'None of it is exotic. It is the ordinary material of a Muslim's week, the same week in which he prays and fasts' — punchy short sentence pairs and 'he' for the believer; A writes 'we' and 'most of us'
'to see, in the marriage and the sleep and the rain, the One whose signs they are' — 'and'-chain and lyrical cadence ending on a grand capitalised 'the One'; A ends on a plain statement
'The Qur'an is not asking for a new set of duties. It is asking whether we perceive...' — not-X-but-Y antithesis as rhetorical device; A says what the Qur'an asks without the staged negation

Epigraph gloss in A's flat style ('These words come from...', 'a prayer many of us recite'), 'Praying, fasting and paying what is due, the wajibat' matches A's listing of the obligations, and the paragraph ends on a plain definitional sentence ('That side of the religion is called ʿirfan'); the stray commas in 'written for us, by the Imams (as), as an endeavour' match A's comma habits.
Word-and-root explanation ('It shares its root with maʿrifah'), Sheikh quoted in three words and glossed, Mutahhari set alongside, plain close linking to the prayer at the head of the page.
'has called for some editorial adaptation' and 'To suit a wider readership' — abstract preface boilerplate; A would say concretely what was changed
'This book is inspired by a lecture series' — soft promotional verb; A would write 'This book is based on'
'for readers who want to go further' — addresses readers as consumers; A keeps the reader implicit in 'we'

Difficulty stated and handed to the Sheikh ('Sheikh Bahmanpour states it himself'), his simile quoted and left to stand, prayers introduced by source and then paraphrased in one flat sentence ('The servant stands there because of need and the prayer gives no other reason for coming').
